title: Onprem Airgapped - artifact delivery, offline licensing, GPU drivers deep dive
customer_attendees: Raj Patel - Head of ML Infra
summary: Deep technical session focused on on-prem air-gapped install logistics: artifact delivery options (SFTP, physical media), offline licensing process and signing window, GPU driver & CUDA version constraints, and runtime knobs (KV cache, batching, quantization) to meet FinSight latency/throughput SLOs.
next_steps: Redwood to provide offline driver bundle + checksums via SFTP (Ava)
Customer to share preferred maintenance window and internal approvers list (Raj)
Redwood SE to send benchmark config and sample scripts (Miguel)
Schedule on-site/remote install pilot for week of 2026-05-04
action_items: Ava: create SFTP account and upload artifact tarball (due: 2026-04-24)
Miguel: prepare benchmark runbook + perf scripts (due: 2026-04-29)
Raj: confirm maintenance window and hardware inventory (due: 2026-04-27)
Leah: share compliance checklist and KMS/HSM contact (due: 2026-04-26)
transcript:
00:00 Ava Chen: ok thanks everyone for joining, we wanted to cover the end to end for an airgap install, artifact delivery, and the offline license flow, and then Miguel will deep dive into drivers and runtime tuning.
00:18 Raj Patel: yep, thanks Ava. we are excited; our main constraints are compliance — everything must be airgapped, no outbound egress from the cluster, and we run on prem in two colo sites.
00:30 Ava Chen: perfect, that's the usual pattern — Miguel, quick context from our side?
00:33 Miguel Torres: sure, hi all. So we'll talk about three buckets: how we get artifacts to you, offline licensing/signing, and GPU/runtime compatibility. i'll also cover KV cache behavior and batching knobs to hit your latency targets.
00:48 Leah Kim: quick Q — for licensing, does Redwood require any outbound call for activation? that's a hard no for us.
00:56 Miguel Torres: good question, by default the offline license flow is designed for zero egress. there's a signed license file we produce after a signed request packet is transferred via sftp or physical media. No outbound calls from the customer cluster.
01:08 Tom Nguyen: and the artifact bundle — is it the full runtime plus drivers, or do we bring our own nvidia package?
01:15 Ava Chen: we can do either. we provide two bundles: 1) Redwood runtime + recommended NVIDIA driver and CUDA libs (tar.gz), or 2) runtime only if you prefer to use your internal driver packaging. For airgap we often deliver the full bundle to reduce variability.
01:34 Raj Patel: what's inside that bundle, concretely?
01:37 Miguel Torres: binaries for our inference runtime, a set of compiled kernels we ship (some are optimized per architecture), the kv cache migration tool, quantization profiles, and optionally the NVIDIA driver rpm/deb + cuda libs. we'll include checksums and a PGP signature.
01:56 Leah Kim: how do you handle mismatches? like we run RHEL 8.6 and our driver baseline is curated by our infra team. We can't just drop a kernel that conflicts.
02:07 Miguel Torres: we provide compatibility matrix in the bundle. For RHEL8 we list supported kernel headers and the superset of driver versions. If your infra team controls the driver, we can just ship runtime and a shim to point to your driver. But if you want the end-to-end tested path, we recommend using our tested driver combo.
02:26 Tom Nguyen: are there licensing keys per node or per cluster? and how is rotation handled?
02:32 Miguel Torres: licensing is per-cluster by default; you get a signed license artifact tied to a cluster ID (we generate the ID from your airgapped install token). For rotation, we support offline license renewal: you generate a renewal request, we sign and hand back a renewed license file. All transfers are operator-initiated.
02:50 Raj Patel: ok good. one of our security folks mentioned KMS integration — we use a YubiHSM and an internal PKI, is that supported?
02:58 Miguel Torres: yes, we support customer-managed keys. For offline deployments you can provide public key material; we produce license blobs signed by that key if you want us to sign with your key, or we can sign with our key and you validate it locally. We also integrate with HSM-backed key stores for encryption-at-rest and TLS.
03:18 Leah Kim: any gotchas around FIPS?
03:21 Miguel Torres: we have a FIPS-compatible build option. it increases the binary size slightly, and some third-party kernels need a recompile. we'll note that in the artifact manifest.
03:31 Ava Chen: Miguel, can you walk through the actual artifact delivery mechanisms you've used?
03:36 Miguel Torres: sure. Mechanisms: SFTP to an airgap dropbox (we can provision a short-lived account), physical shipping (encrypted USB or imprint image on SSD) via courier, or customer-initiated scp from a pre-staged internal server. For larger sites we also use an rsync-over-ssh pattern via a secure bastion. All bundles are signed and checksummed.
03:56 Raj Patel: what about checksums and verification steps? we need a deterministic validation script for our runbook.
04:03 Miguel Torres: bundle includes sha256 checksums + PGP signatures. We provide a verification script that checks signatures against the Redwood public key (or your public key if you requested). We'll also include a small validation container that runs basic smoke tests.
04:20 Leah Kim: sounds good. about GPU drivers — we've had issues where driver mismatches killed the nodes. does Redwood have a recommended driver matrix for A100 and L40?
04:30 Miguel Torres: yes: for A100 we recommend NVIDIA driver 525.x with CUDA 11.8; for L40 we recommend 535.x with CUDA 12.1. That said, we have tested quantized kernels on both stacks. We'll include prebuilt kernel modules for 525.x and 535.x in the bundle.
04:50 Tom Nguyen: do you support proprietary nvidia licensing? some vendors require you to accept a license on install which is hard in airgap.
04:57 Miguel Torres: we provide the driver package and legal notice in the bundle, but your infra team will need to accept any vendor terms per your policy. For fully locked down installs we can provide an installation script that timestamps acceptance into your internal audit log file for traceability.
05:12 Ava Chen: switching to runtime performance — Raj, can you remind us of the perf goals?
05:17 Raj Patel: target p95 latency of 350ms for 1k token sequences on our L40 nodes, throughput of ~120 concurrent streams across 8 GPUs. cost isn't as big an issue as latency; we need deterministic tails.
05:29 Miguel Torres: ok that's helpful. Two primary levers: KV cache configuration and batching policy. KV cache warmup and cache locality are critical for long sequences. We have an adaptive prefix cache that keeps hot KV shards in memory.
05:43 Leah Kim: any memory overhead we should budget for the KV cache?
05:46 Miguel Torres: yes, default KV cache for long-context models can be ~0.5 to 1.2 GiB per concurrent stream depending on sequence length and hidden size. For your L40 profile we'd suggest reserving 40-50GB of host+GPU memory across the pod for KV operations.
06:04 Tom Nguyen: you mentioned continuous batching — how does that affect tail latency?
06:08 Miguel Torres: continuous batching aggregates micro-requests to improve throughput with bounded latency. We expose two modes: low-latency mode (batch sizes capped, max wait 5ms) and high-throughput (aggressive coalescing). For p95 tail we recommend low-latency mode with explicit batch caps and per-route latency SLOs.
06:26 Raj Patel: how deterministic is the batching? we need reproducible p95 numbers for our SLA.
06:31 Miguel Torres: with the low-latency mode and reserved GPU pool (your Dedicated layout), the variance drops considerably. We'll run internal bench runs and share a 95/99 profile. Also we expose a token-level cost and latency breakdown in the console — though in airgap you get an offline export of those metrics.
06:51 Leah Kim: quantization — we plan to use INT8 for some workloads. do you support mixed precision quantization? and what about generation quality regressions?
06:59 Miguel Torres: yes, we support int8 and 4-bit quantization profiles; we also have dynamic mixed-precision paths. For quality we ship evaluation prompts and an eval harness. We recommend starting with 8-bit and running A/B evals vs FP16 for your critical prompt sets. We also have rollback profiles if regressions occur.
07:20 Tom Nguyen: are quantized kernels included in the artifact bundle? or are they generated at install time?
07:25 Miguel Torres: quantized kernels are precompiled for the common architectures; for custom chipsets we provide a quantize-and-compile tool in the bundle that runs offline. That tool can be slow (compilation can take hours) so we prebuild when possible.
07:39 Raj Patel: can you explain the KV cache eviction policy — we have long context chats across many users and we need fairness, no single tenant hogging.
07:48 Miguel Torres: eviction is tiered: hot prefixes pinned by heuristic (recent access), per-tenant caps, and LRU across lower-priority shards. You can tune caps per route; for multi-tenant fairness we advise per-tenant quotas in the platform config.
08:03 Leah Kim: back to drivers: do you require specific kernel modules? or is everything in user-space?
08:08 Miguel Torres: mostly user-space; the NVIDIA driver is kernel-level and required for GPU access. We ship userspace libs and optionally the driver installer. Our runtime doesn't require custom kernel modules for normal operation, but some of our optimized kernels load via the nvidia-ucm path — that's standard for NVIDIA.
08:24 Tom Nguyen: one of our nodes is older — Ampere but early firmware. is firmware compatibility something you validate?
08:29 Miguel Torres: yes, we validate against firmware baseline in the compatibility matrix. If firmware is older, performance regressions can occur; we'll flag that and recommend an update.
08:37 Raj Patel: any recommended observability during install for us to capture perf regressions?
08:42 Miguel Torres: we provide a perf agent that collects token-level latencies, batch sizes, GPU utilization, and KV cache hit rates. In airgap this runs locally and we provide a guidance sheet to extract the metrics and send a sanitized report to Redwood if you'd like assistance.
08:58 Ava Chen: quick pause — Leah, any compliance blockers we haven't covered?
09:02 Leah Kim: mainly the egress and chain of custody. the physical media option is preferable for some workloads. we need signed manifests and chain of custody for the shipped SSD.
09:11 Miguel Torres: chain of custody we can support, including tamper-evident seals and signed manifests.
09:17 Tom Nguyen: how big are the bundles typically? we have limited airgap transfer windows.
09:22 Miguel Torres: runtime + drivers + kernels ~ 4-12GB depending on whether we include CUDA libs, quantized kernels, and debug symbols. We can produce a minimal bundle (~1.2GB) that excludes debug and optional kernels.
09:35 Raj Patel: and incremental updates? we don't want full re-transfer every month.
09:39 Miguel Torres: we support delta patches using rsync diffs and a manifest-based patcher. For airgap physical media, we can provide patch kits which are much smaller.
09:48 Leah Kim: about the license file again — what metadata is inside? expiration, node count?
09:53 Miguel Torres: metadata includes cluster ID, node counts or GPU counts, expiration, and feature flags (e.g., Dedicated, KV cache size caps). It's opaque and signed; we also provide a human-readable summary in the admin UI/offline manifest.
10:07 Ava Chen: Miguel, can you walk through a sample install flow step-by-step?
10:11 Miguel Torres: yes: 1) Redwood generates artifact bundle and uploads to SFTP or ships physical media. 2) Customer operator imports bundle, runs verify script (signature + sha256) and smoke container. 3) Customer runs install script which packages runtime into a container registry on-prem (airgap registry) or directly extracts to an operator path. 4) Customer runs license-request tool (produces CSR-like packet), sends to Redwood via SFTP or courier. 5) Redwood returns signed license file. 6) Customer installs license and starts the runtime. 7) Run perf harness and share logs for tuning.
10:41 Tom Nguyen: is the license-request format human-auditable? we have to store it for audit.
10:45 Miguel Torres: yes it's a json+signature file; we can output a redacted version for your audit store.
10:52 Raj Patel: when would we need an online handshake? any cases?
10:55 Miguel Torres: only in specific optional telemetry cases — but for your compliance profile we can disable telemetry entirely. All admin telemetry can be exported manually.
11:03 Leah Kim: what about security of the SFTP account? ephemeral creds?
11:07 Miguel Torres: yes, SFTP accounts are short lived and we recommend key-based auth. We'll create an account per-transfer and rotate creds afterward.
11:14 Ava Chen: Miguel, perf tips — for p95 350ms, any kernel-level flags or CUDA tweaks?
11:19 Miguel Torres: a few: set the GPU persistence mode on, tune cuda context prewarm (we'll provide a script), align batch sizes to model I/O to avoid tail fragmentation, and pin memory for token streams. Also disable unnecessary cgroup throttles on the operator pods.
11:36 Tom Nguyen: do you have a recommended orchestration topology? like per-gpu pods vs shared pods?
11:41 Miguel Torres: for low tail latency, per-GPU dedicated containers (one shard per GPU) tends to be most deterministic. Shared multi-GPU pods increase throughput but can increase variance.
11:52 Raj Patel: what about autoscaling? in airgap we want static pools but some burst capability would help.
11:59 Miguel Torres: we support scheduled burst windows via reserved burst nodes; you can pre-stage additional nodes and flip routes via the control plane. In fully airgapped customers you can control this via manual activation or an internal orchestrator.
12:11 Leah Kim: any troubleshooting we should prepare for? failures we've seen?
12:15 Miguel Torres: common issues: driver/kernel mismatch leading to GPU hangs, incorrect cuda libs causing symbol errors, and permissions on the license file. Our install runbook includes checks for dmesg, nvidia-smi, and a small trial generation to verify end-to-end.
12:31 Ava Chen: time check — we've covered a bunch; Miguel one last thing — benchmarks you'll send?
12:36 Miguel Torres: yes i'll attach a benchmark config that mirrors your target: 1k tokens, p95 profiles, 8 GPU pool. It includes the batch cap settings we discussed, KV cache warmup script, and the smoke harness.
12:48 Raj Patel: good. Tom, any internal blockers from infra?
12:51 Tom Nguyen: we'll need to carve a maintenance window, and Leah will need the compliance docs. other than that, good.
12:58 Leah Kim: please include the chain of custody form and a sample SFTP policy in the docs.
13:04 Ava Chen: noted; we'll include those. wrap up in the next 5 min with concrete recaps.
13:11 Miguel Torres: Recap: Redwood to provide full artifact bundle (or minimal if requested) with drivers and quantized kernels, checksums, PGP signatures, and verification scripts. Offline license flow: customer produces request packet -> SFTP/courier -> Redwood signs and returns license. Perf: use low-latency batching, per-GPU pods, KV cache warmup, and specific driver versions for L40/A100.
13:35 Raj Patel: Next steps — we will confirm hardware inventory and maintenance window; Redwood to upload bundle and bench scripts.
13:41 Ava Chen: thanks all. we'll follow up with the SFTP creds and an upload by 2026-04-24 as discussed.
13:48 Tom Nguyen: thanks everyone.
13:50 Leah Kim: thanks, bye.
13:52 End of recording.
